Muru. Graham Dumpleton started mod_wsgi 20 years ago, and has been thinking about the ideal way to serve Python web applications in production ever since.
Muru is his new, AI-assisted Rust server that aims to provide the best possible tools for running ASGI and WSGI Python apps both in development and production.
As he did with wrapture, he's been publishing an extraordinarily detailed account of the project as he works on it - as part of his development process.
Here's everything he's published so far, all in the last three weeks:
2026-11-04 — Twenty years of mod_wsgi, and what comes next
2026-11-05 — A first look at Muru
2026-11-07 — Muru: looking inside the workers
2026-11-08 — Muru: how it fits together
2026-11-09 — Muru: import once, fork many

2026-11-17 — Muru: scaling to zero

2026-11-19 — Muru: noticing and responding
2026-11-20 — Muru: a toolbar on every page
2026-11-21 — Muru: tracing in the toolbar
2026-11-22 — Muru: when lazy imports help
That post about AI as a lifestyle choice is particularly worth a read:

The AI may be doing a lot of the work on the surface, but deciding what isn't good enough yet is still down to me, and twenty years of getting things wrong with mod_wsgi turns out to be useful for that. I am prepared to put in the hard work to keep polishing Muru until it is something I would trust, and something you would too.

The secret to writing good code1 is to avoid catastrophic mistakes. Many engineers think about programming as if the goal is to have brilliant insights, but they’re wrong. If you don’t blunder, you will win.

Many other domains are like this. If you can play chess without ever hanging pieces, you will win against almost any2 opponent. If you are very good at returning tennis balls, you will beat most players even if you never hit a winner. People are really bad at internalizing this. They think that being good at chess means finding brilliant tactical combinations, or that being good at tennis means crushing balls into the corner of the court, or that being a good programmer means discovering beautiful new abstractions. Not so! All of those things are valuable, but they are not the main thing. The main thing is to avoid catastrophic mistakes.

The reason programming is like this is that it is impossible to build a durable winning advantage. In basketball, if you are up 99-1, the worst consequence of a blunder is still being up 99-4. However, in programming, one blunder can turn an elegant codebase into a janky one. For instance, consider these blunders:
Introducing a parallel system to perform the same task
Introducing a second source of truth for some key piece of data
Turning a safe sync operation into a delicate async one
Adding new subtle points of failure
Complicating a key interface

The cardinal sins here are inconsistency and introducing unnecessary requirements3. Even a little bit of inconsistency is dangerous because it breaks trust: instead of assuming your code works the sensible way, engineers must now go looking for surprises.

Unnecessary requirements are dangerous for two reasons. First, they’re sticky. When you’re implementing a new requirement, you have the context to decide whether it’s necessary or not. If you see one in the codebase, you must assume it’s necessary unless you’re willing to spend a bunch of time researching. So requirements tend to remain in codebases long after they could be removed. Second, they often interrelate in dangerous ways: if your codebase supports X, then you must consider how each new feature will interact with X. This combinatorial explosion is what makes working in large codebases so hard4.
When you’re writing code, you must at all costs try to:
Identify where your task could fit most normally into the current codebase
Trim your task down into the smallest set of requirements that you can

In fact, you should be so focused on this — on avoiding blunders — that you don’t really have mental energy to be worrying about cool tricks or “extra credit” features. As with shipping projects, if you find yourself thinking things like “oh, I could implement it with this clever pattern”, this is a warning sign: you are likely becoming distracted from the main thing, and you risk blundering.

You don’t have to be clever to do great programming work. In fact, sometimes cleverness can be a disadvantage. What you need is attention to detail and a laser focus on what actually matters: avoiding blunders by maintaining consistency and skipping unnecessary requirements.

As usual on this blog, I am primarily talking about working on large commercial codebases with big teams: “impure engineering” in my terminology. This advice may not apply if you’re doing other kinds of work. Of course all of this applies whether you’re writing code by hand or driving an AI agent.
↩

My guess (it’s surprisingly hard to research) is that not ever blundering would get you around a 1600 or 1700 chess rating: strong enough to win almost every game against casual players.
↩

Current coding agents are pretty good at consistency — about as good as humans — but are far worse at avoiding unnecessary requirements, unfortunately.
↩

I wrote about this in depth in Wicked features.
↩

blocks.text: While on holiday in Vilnius, I realised my beard was getting too long for the impending heatwave. I popped into literally the first barber I found and asked them to shave my mane back down to summer length.

As the chair reclined leaving me supine, the barber placed a moist towelette over my eyes and proceeded to start steaming my beard while gently brushing it. As his firm hands vigourously started massaging various unguents into my luxurious facial hair, all I could think was "Am I enjoying this?"

I had little choice but to lie back and let the professional work his magic. I got the hot towel, the cold towel, the head and shoulder massage, various scented pomades, and a selection of razors carefully whisked against my whiskers.

I don't think I enjoyed it. Obviously it is nice to smell nice, and it was helpful to have someone else use professional tools to make me look neat & tidy. I don't mind when I go into a cheap coiffeuse and am shaved in five minutes - but this was close to an hour of being pampered.

I didn't have a visceral reaction or a complete meltdown. At best I'd say I tolerated it.  I felt much the same when I went to get my hair dyed. Is it that I don't like strangers touching me? Do I think I'm not worthy of a little pampering and indulgence?

By contrast, I went for dental surgery a couple of years ago and found it to be a weirdly pleasant sensation. Again, I was laid flat out, my eyes were closed, and I had a small team of professionals prodding and poking at my body. For an instant, I felt both completely vulnerable and incredibly safe. I understood why some people fake medical issues and place themselves in the hands of surgeons.
To have a dedicated professional fix you feels calming and therapeutic.
Perhaps I regard my various hairs as æsthetic fripperies? To give in to vanity is unworthy and unbecoming - but to succumb to failings of the flesh is merely mortal.

I have no problems with opticians and proctologists performing their intimate procedures on me. I can't stand getting massaged, but found physiotherapy rather pleasant. The thought of getting a pedicure fills me with horror.
Is there any difference between a physio poking at my foot in order to fix it and a pedicurist sculpting my nails and filing my calluses?
My brain is obviously weird and I need to buy myself a travel-suitable beard trimmer.

blocks.text: Strictly speaking, the proper mouse for the Tandy 1000, at least the early models, was the TRS-80 color mouse. But it’s not your only option and arguably isn’t your best option. In this blog post, I’ll explain some alternatives, including the one I use.
The TRS-80 color mouse

The TRS-80 color mouse, part number 26-3025,  takes its name from the TRS-80 Color Computer. The mouse isn’t very colorful though. It came in jet black with a single red button. Maybe they should have called it the TRS-80 goth mouse. Its squared-off design is also about as ergonomic as it is colorful.

One could also argue it’s not really a proper mouse. It uses a pair of potentiometers, so it works more like an analog joystick than like a mouse. It’s also not compatible with other more conventional mice, so you will have to get Tandy’s driver in order to use it.
But since it plugs into the joystick port, it will work on any early Tandy 1000, even unexpanded models.
But I opted to go a different route, because the TRS-80 color mouse is hard to find and expensive.
Tandy/Radio Shack Serial mice

But if you can equip your Tandy 1000 with an RS-232 serial port, you can use any 9-pin RS-232 serial mouse with it. A Microsoft Dove bar mouse is a reasonably good fit, period-correct, easy to find, and inexpensive. An early Logitech mouse would also be a good fit.

But what if you like things to match? You’re in luck. Radio Shack sold Tandy-branded mice. The most period-correct choice would be catalog number 25-1040D, but it’s also harder to find. Later, Radio Shack sold Tandy-branded Logitech mice, such as catalog number 25-2001. They look exactly like the Logitech mice that companies like Compaq and Dell supplied with their machines, but they have the Tandy logo on them. The going rate on these is around $25.

After Tandy left the computer business and Radio Shack started selling IBM and Compaq computers instead, they still continued to sell computer accessories. These often had Radio Shack branding instead of Tandy. A Radio Shack RS-232 mouse such as catalog number 26-326 is reasonably inexpensive today, and looks the part next to a Tandy 1000, even though it’s from the wrong decade. Prices on these were over $40 during the pandemic but you can pick one up today for closer to $15.

The advantage with a later serial mouse is they will work with pretty much any mouse driver you want to use. Tandy 1000s tend to be a bit memory challenged, so being able to use ctmouse, which only needs 6K, is a nice advantage. The later Radio Shack branded mice are still relabeled Logitech units, with slightly updated styling in keeping for the time when it was produced.
This blog post is part of my series about Tandy and Radio Shack. Click or tap for the index.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

In the previous post on this
topic,
we’ve seen how the Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS) and transform
(DTFT) are used to analyze infinite-duration periodic and non-periodic
discrete signals. Now, it’s time to turn to realistic digital signal
processing where signals are not only discrete, but also finite in
duration.
Analyzing signal samples

Suppose we have  samples of a signal - it’s a list of 
numbers:

We want to analyze the frequencies present in this signal; in other
words, to find the coefficients in a series of complex exponentials that
reconstructs the signal. One option is to assume that  is an
infinite domain signal with zero values outside our  samples, and then
compute its DTFT:

However, this is a continuous function of frequency , so it’s
difficult compute on an actual computer; we cannot evaluate and
store it for all , so we have to choose which  to compute it
for. We'll soon see how this choice is made.

But there's an alternative way to look at the problem. We only have 
samples of the signal , so we can assume they represent a single period
of a periodic signal. And in that case, we can use DTFS; recall that the
coefficients of the series are:

As we’ve seen in the post on the DTFS,
this series can be used to
reconstruct a discrete, periodic signal precisely. Since our signal
 is finite and we assume it’s just one period of a periodic
signal, it means we can also reconstruct  precisely using a
DTFS.

This is the main insight behind the Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT).
First, by convention [1] we define:
And then:

This is called the Discrete Fourier Transform of . The term
transform may be a bit puzzling here - after all, we’re just using the
series coefficients - so isn’t it more proper to just say series?
Perhaps, though in mathematics a transform has a pretty general
meaning of "a mapping that takes a mathematical object and produces
another object"; in that sense, "transform" is proper here because we
take an object -  and produce another object - .

Moreover, DFT and DTFT are intimately related. Recall how we said
earlier that the DTFT is tricky to compute because  is a
continuous variable? Well, the DFT gives us a way to sample that
variable into the discrete domain:

So the DFT can be seen as exactly  equally spaced samples of
the DTFT.
Computing the DFT

Since the goal of this post is specifically to demonstrate computable
methods of applying Fourier analysis to discrete digital signals, here’s
the Python code to calculate the DFT of a signal:

def dft(x):
    """Return X[k] = sum_n x[n] exp(-2 pi i k n / N)."""
    N = len(x)
    n = np.arange(N)
    X = np.empty(N, dtype=complex)
    for k in range(N):
        weights = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * k * n / N)
        X[k] = np.sum(x * weights)
    return X

It shouldn’t be hard to see the correspondence between this code and the
mathematical formula for . Python’s Numpy code is vectorized
by default, so the weights array is computed in whole for every
k (because n is an array of indices ).
DFT and the complex roots of unity

In my earlier post on the complex roots of
unity,
we’ve seen how powers of the roots of unity form an orthogonal basis for
. Now let’s show the beautiful theoretical
connection between this fact and the DFT.
Recall that the -th roots of unity can be written as:

Since all  are just powers of , we
can write them as:
The conjugates of the roots of unity are roots of unity themselves:

With  being the same as , so when we
enumerate all the roots of unity, we’re also enumerating their
conjugates, just in a reversed order.

With that in mind, let’s denote [2] ,
and examine the sequence:

The vectors formed by (element-wise) raising  to integer powers
from  to  can be collected into a matrix:

In the roots of unity
post,
we’ve proven that the rows of this matrix form an orthogonal basis over
. In other words, any vector in 
can be represented as a linear combination of the rows of .

I hope you can see where this is going! Let’s consider the signal
 as a column vector in . The DFT of
 can be computed by multiplying  by the matrix
:

Take a minute to convince yourself this is true, by working through the
multiplication for a specific row , e.g.  is
computed via row-column multiplication the third row (counting from 0)
of  and .

Our  is called the Fourier Matrix or the DFT Matrix.
Previously we’ve seen Python code that directly computes the DFT; here’s
a version that does this via the matrix multiplication approach:

def dft_matrix(N):
    """Construct F[k, n] = W_N**(k*n), where W_N = exp(-2 pi i / N)."""
    # W_N is a primitive N-th root of unity: W_N**N = 1.
    # Its powers give all N roots of z**N - 1 = 0.
    root = np.exp(-2j * np.pi / N)
    indices = np.arange(N)
    # Rows correspond to frequency bins k; columns to sample indices n.
    exponents = np.outer(indices, indices)
    return root**exponents

def dft_via_matrix(x):
    """Compute the DFT as F @ x with the Fourier matrix"""
    return dft_matrix(len(x)) @ x

More than the computational convenience though, there’s theoretical
elegance here. Back when we were discussing the continuous Fourier
series,
we’ve seen how the trigonometric functions (or - equivalently - complex
exponentials) form an orthogonal basis for square integrable functions.

Here, we see a similar linear algebra connection in discrete time - the
vectors formed from powers of complex roots of unity form an orthogonal
basis in  and can thus be used to represent any
sequence of  complex values.

Which brings us to the next topic: reconstructing a signal from its DFT
representation.
Inverse DFT: reconstructing the signal

There are two equivalent approaches to find the inverse DFT - the
formula we can use to reconstruct  given . The
first approach is going back to DTFS, where the reconstruction formula
is:

This is the Inverse Discrete Fourier Transform formula.

Let’s examine the other approach now, because it uses our linear algebra
interpretation in an enlightening way.

Recall the Fourier matrix , and consider  - the same
matrix where every element is the conjugate of the corresponding element
of . If:
Then:

We have seen in the roots of unity
post
that this amounts to:
In other words:

Where  is the identity matrix. Since  is a square
matrix, any matrix that multiplies with it to give the identity is its
inverse:
Recall that in vector form:
Therefore:
With our definition of :
And in sum form:

Which is the same reconstruction formula we obtained from the DTFS. In
mathematics, it’s always a good sign when we obtain the same result
using different methods!

The linear algebra interpretation here is clear: the vectors formed by
the powers of roots of unity form an orthogonal basis over
. Therefore, every vector 
can be represented as a linear combination of these vectors. Moreover,
this transformation is invertible, and the original vector can be
reconstructed by left-multiplying its DFT vector  by

Example

It’s time for a fully worked example; the entire Python code for this
example is available on GitHub;
read through its main function, which is well
commented.
In code, this is just an array of numbers:

Calculating the DFT of this signal using the code shown earlier produces
the following values; remember that  consists of complex
numbers, so we represent them as a magnitude-phase pair. Phase is only
shown for nonzero coefficients, because the phase of zero is
undefined [3]:

Obviously, we’d get exactly the same numbers by using the matrix
multiplication method of computing the DFT. And to reconstruct the
signal, we multiply by the computed IDFT matrix to get the original
signal back. The reconstruction matches the original signal precisely,
with any differences being attributable to floating point round-off.
Efficiently computing the DFT

The sample code
contains another method of computing the DFT of
this signal - by calling NumPy’s
fft.fft
function. This refers to the Fast Fourier Transform, which is
considered to be one of the most important algorithms of the 20th
century. By exploiting the structure of the Fourier matrix ,
FFT computes the product  in 
operations, compared with  for direct matrix-vector
multiplication. I plan to cover how this works in a future post.
Appendix: spectral leakage

Looking carefully at the signal used in the Example section above, we
see that it’s actually one full cycle out of a sampled triangle wave.
This is convenient, because repeating the block reproduces the original
triangle wave. But what happens when the samples cover only part of the
cycle?
Take for example just the first 10 samples of the triangle wave:

If we naively extend this signal periodically, things won’t line up
(there will be a jump at the end of every cycle). We can still calculate
its DFT, of course; these are the coefficients we’ll get:

While the coefficients still come in conjugate pairs (because the
samples are real), the original triangle’s frequencies no longer
coincide with the DFT’s frequency bins, so their contributions spread
across multiple bins. This is called spectral
leakage.

By applying the IDFT we can still reconstruct the original 10-sample
signal perfectly! So if all we need is reconstruction, spectral leakage
isn’t an issue; but if we’re doing frequency analysis, it skews the
situation somewhat, adding frequencies that didn’t really exist in the
underlying triangle wave - just to account for the discontinuity. In
real-world signal processing, such issues are usually addressed by
applying special window functions to the signal after sampling - these
help alleviate leakage by tapering the signal close to zero at the
edges.

meaning of "a mapping that takes a mathematical object and produces
another object"; in that sense, "transform" is proper here because we
take an object -  and produce another object - .

Moreover, DFT and DTFT are intimately related. Recall how we said
earlier that the DTFT is tricky to compute because  is a
continuous variable? Well, the DFT gives us a way to sample that
variable into the discrete domain:

So the DFT can be seen as exactly  equally spaced samples of
the DTFT.
Computing the DFT

Since the goal of this post is specifically to demonstrate computable
methods of applying Fourier analysis to discrete digital signals, here’s
the Python code to calculate the DFT of a signal:

def dft(x):
    """Return X[k] = sum_n x[n] exp(-2 pi i k n / N)."""
    N = len(x)
    n = np.arange(N)
    X = np.empty(N, dtype=complex)
    for k in range(N):
        weights = np.exp(-2j * np.pi * k * n / N)
        X[k] = np.sum(x * weights)
    return X

It shouldn’t be hard to see the correspondence between this code and the
mathematical formula for . Python’s Numpy code is vectorized
by default, so the weights array is computed in whole for every
k (because n is an array of indices ).
DFT and the complex roots of unity

In my earlier post on the complex roots of
unity,
we’ve seen how powers of the roots of unity form an orthogonal basis for

connection between this fact and the DFT.
Recall that the -th roots of unity can be written as:

With  being the same as , so when we
enumerate all the roots of unity, we’re also enumerating their

With that in mind, let’s denote [2] ,

from  to  can be collected into a matrix:

In the roots of unity
post,
we’ve proven that the rows of this matrix form an orthogonal basis over

can be represented as a linear combination of the rows of .

I hope you can see where this is going! Let’s consider the signal

Take a minute to convince yourself this is true, by working through the
multiplication for a specific row , e.g.  is

Our  is called the Fourier Matrix or the DFT Matrix.
Previously we’ve seen Python code that directly computes the DFT; here’s
a version that does this via the matrix multiplication approach:

def dft_matrix(N):
    """Construct F[k, n] = W_N**(k*n), where W_N = exp(-2 pi i / N)."""
    # W_N is a primitive N-th root of unity: W_N**N = 1.
    # Its powers give all N roots of z**N - 1 = 0.
    root = np.exp(-2j * np.pi / N)
    indices = np.arange(N)
    # Rows correspond to frequency bins k; columns to sample indices n.
    exponents = np.outer(indices, indices)
    return root**exponents

def dft_via_matrix(x):
    """Compute the DFT as F @ x with the Fourier matrix"""
    return dft_matrix(len(x)) @ x

More than the computational convenience though, there’s theoretical
elegance here. Back when we were discussing the continuous Fourier
series,
we’ve seen how the trigonometric functions (or - equivalently - complex
exponentials) form an orthogonal basis for square integrable functions.

Here, we see a similar linear algebra connection in discrete time - the
vectors formed from powers of complex roots of unity form an orthogonal
basis in  and can thus be used to represent any
sequence of  complex values.

representation.

The linear algebra interpretation here is clear: the vectors formed by

Example

It’s time for a fully worked example; the entire Python code for this
example is available on GitHub;
read through its main function, which is well

In code, this is just an array of numbers:

Calculating the DFT of this signal using the code shown earlier produces
the following values; remember that  consists of complex
numbers, so we represent them as a magnitude-phase pair. Phase is only
shown for nonzero coefficients, because the phase of zero is
undefined [3]:

Obviously, we’d get exactly the same numbers by using the matrix
multiplication method of computing the DFT. And to reconstruct the
signal, we multiply by the computed IDFT matrix to get the original
signal back. The reconstruction matches the original signal precisely,
with any differences being attributable to floating point round-off.
Efficiently computing the DFT

The sample code
contains another method of computing the DFT of
this signal - by calling NumPy’s
fft.fft
function. This refers to the Fast Fourier Transform, which is
considered to be one of the most important algorithms of the 20th
century. By exploiting the structure of the Fourier matrix ,
FFT computes the product  in 
operations, compared with  for direct matrix-vector
multiplication. I plan to cover how this works in a future post.
Appendix: spectral leakage

Looking carefully at the signal used in the Example section above, we
see that it’s actually one full cycle out of a sampled triangle wave.
This is convenient, because repeating the block reproduces the original
triangle wave. But what happens when the samples cover only part of the
cycle?
Take for example just the first 10 samples of the triangle wave:

If we naively extend this signal periodically, things won’t line up
(there will be a jump at the end of every cycle). We can still calculate
its DFT, of course; these are the coefficients we’ll get:

While the coefficients still come in conjugate pairs (because the
samples are real), the original triangle’s frequencies no longer
coincide with the DFT’s frequency bins, so their contributions spread
across multiple bins. This is called spectral
leakage.

By applying the IDFT we can still reconstruct the original 10-sample
signal perfectly! So if all we need is reconstruction, spectral leakage
isn’t an issue; but if we’re doing frequency analysis, it skews the
situation somewhat, adding frequencies that didn’t really exist in the
underlying triangle wave - just to account for the discontinuity. In
real-world signal processing, such issues are usually addressed by
applying special window functions to the signal after sampling - these
help alleviate leakage by tapering the signal close to zero at the
edges.

blocks.text: "You can't outsource accountability". But it feels like that's what's happening when a disclosure notice refers to "an incident being at a third party", as though somehow that makes it better. It feels like the intent is to deflect responsibility, but ultimately, accountability remains with the party we entrusted our data to in the first place. It's also ultimately them who needs to decide whether to disclose the incident, so in the case of Optimizely this week, even though it's clearly their fault, it's up to the likes of Norwegian Airlines to decide whether they're contacting impacted individuals. And then, in their case, they haven't named the third party anyway! Strange times, I reckon.
